summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. In February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia, restricting trans people's use of public bathrooms; the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Ica has no recorded trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern. The national framework applies unchanged in the department, and the bathroom restriction binds public and private premises throughout it.

The congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved on 20 February 2025 a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions cover custody, medical attention, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, and the text bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The bills were triggered by a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory, warning that access would depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved the text and exempted it from a second vote. Article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for the listed exceptions. The legal analysis of Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte for IDEHPUCP, the human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, holds that the provision violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. IDEHPUCP describes the package as legalised discrimination against trans access to public space and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private as well as public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, covered by Agencia Presentes in July 2024, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, of which 12 were trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with multiple gunshots or stabbings. The 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denunciations in 2020. The report recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. These figures cover Peru as a whole rather than Ica. A separate 2024 report found hate crimes rising in the country with trans women most affected; its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the regional human-rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the court through the regional human-rights commission.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. That binding regional standard sits directly against the Peruvian bathroom statute, and IDEHPUCP's constitutional challenge is framed in the same terms.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Under-recording is a standing caveat on the violence figures. The observatory's totals are drawn from public reporting and denunciations, and the co-author of the 2024 hate-crime report states that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry, so the true incidence in Ica is likely higher than any official count.

Regional comparison is unflattering. With Paraguay and Guyana, Peru is one of only three South American countries whose hate-crime law carries no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage, which removes the charge a trans visitor or resident would otherwise bring after an assault.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ica live under the national bathroom statute with no local ordinance to soften or widen it. Public premises, gyms, malls and workplaces in the department apply the 'biological sex' test, and a consumer-protection body has already dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, so the administrative complaint route has produced no relief.

Inclusive signage is banned, which affects local businesses, community organisations and schools that use wording such as 'women in their diversity'. Article 4 of the April 2025 law additionally restricts media and advertising content, and the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years, exposing local publishers, artists and educators working on identity themes to prosecution.

Healthcare in the department improved on paper in June 2024, when national health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance, a change that residents can invoke in clinical settings. A July 2025 ruling by a Lima constitutional court, obtained after an activist challenge, struck down an anti-equality decree and gives residents a further domestic legal argument.

Residents have no hate-crime statute covering anti-LGBT motive, following the 2017 repeal, and must instead rely on ordinary assault provisions. Police conduct is the site of the country's worst documented case: three officers were sentenced in December 2025 to 17 years for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, the first Peruvian conviction for a crime motivated by sexual discrimination.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records trans-specific enforcement, arrests, complaints or violence in Ica itself. Whether local police, municipal inspectors or private security in Ica apply identity-document checks at restrooms is unresolved and not sourced; the only documented enforcement example is a Lima-based gym complaint that a consumer-protection body dismissed.

The homicide and rights-violation totals are national. No breakdown by department exists in the inventory, so Ica's share of the 54 killings and 170 violation cases recorded for 2020-2023 is unknown, and the Rubí Torres Silvano case occurred in Lima.

The final law number, promulgation date and official text of the April 2025 package are not sourced here; the inventory establishes committee approval on 20 February 2025 and plenary approval with exemption from second vote on 2 April 2025. Whether the statute has been challenged before the Inter-American Court, as distinct from the domestic constitutional ruling of July 2025, is unresolved.

Gianna Camacho's statement that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms is an activist claim reported by Infobae Perú and is not corroborated in the inventory by an official study.
